Enteral Nutrition Decisions and the Challenge of Early Prognostication Accurate characterization of swallowing impairment is particularly important because it informs one of the most consequential decisions made during acute stroke hospitalization: how nutrition, hydration, and medication administration will be managed during recovery. Dysphagia frequently limits safe oral intake during the early post-stroke period, yet prolonged inadequate nutrition and hydration are associated with worse functional outcomes, increased morbidity, and increased mortality [ 22 – 25 ]. Medication administration may also depend on enteral access, creating additional pressure to establish reliable feeding routes early.

Because G-tubes can theoretically be removed if swallowing function recovers, placement is often viewed as a relatively low-risk or reversible intervention during periods of prognostic uncertainty. However, the practical consequences of G-tube placement frequently extend well beyond the acute hospitalization period. Once placed, G-tubes may persist because of limited reassessment, barriers to repeat swallowing imaging, and challenges accessing rehabilitation services. As a result, decisions initially intended to support short-term recovery may ultimately influence long-term swallowing management and quality of life.

Decisions regarding enteral nutrition can be complicated by the highly dynamic nature of swallowing recovery after stroke. Meaningful improvement may occur within days or weeks, with continued recovery extending months beyond hospitalization [ 39 – 45 ]. As a result, clinicians are often asked to make long-term nutritional management decisions during a period of substantial physiologic uncertainty, before the patient’s ultimate swallowing trajectory can be confidently determined. Although several prognostic tools, such as the Predictive Swallowing Score (PRESS), have been developed to support feeding tube decision-making, none have been validated using swallowing imaging, and the variables included across models vary considerably [ 86 – 89 ]. Accurately predicting long-term enteral nutrition, therefore, remains difficult.

Current guidelines generally support G-tube placement only when prolonged inability to swallow safely is anticipated [ 56 ], with existing recommendations favoring nasogastric (NG) tube feeding during the initial weeks after stroke before considering long-term enteral access [ 9 , 90 ]. However, real-world practice frequently diverges from these recommendations. Acute care length of stay has progressively shortened, often resulting in discharge timelines that precede recommended waiting periods for G-tube decisions [ 46 – 48 ]. Acute care clinicians are, therefore, frequently asked to determine long-term enteral nutrition needs before the trajectory of swallowing recovery becomes apparent.

Systems-level pressures further complicate these decisions. Many post-acute facilities remain reluctant to accept patients with NG tubes because of staffing concerns, radiographic confirmation requirements, reimbursement limitations, and care coordination challenges, should G-tube placement ultimately become necessary [ 3 , 47 , 48 , 50 ]. Consequently, acute care hospitals often assume responsibility for determining whether patients should undergo G-tube placement prior to discharge. In practice, this means that decisions regarding enteral nutrition are often driven not only by swallowing prognosis and supplemental nutritional needs, but also by discharge logistics and post-acute placement barriers.

One potential strategy for reducing this prognostic pressure would be greater acceptance of patients with NG tubes across post-acute care settings [ 91 , 92 ]. Although such an approach would require infrastructure and workflow changes, it could allow additional time for swallowing recovery and reassessment while maintaining closer alignment with existing guideline recommendations regarding the timing of G-tube decisions. Importantly, this approach would also create opportunities for repeat swallowing imaging and more individualized prognostication before committing patients to long-term nutrition access.

The consequences of these decisions often extend far beyond the acute hospitalization period. Longitudinal outcome studies demonstrate that many stroke survivors experience substantial swallowing recovery after discharge, including recovery sufficient to permit feeding tube removal [ 53 , 86 , 93 ]. Even when enteral nutrition is medically necessary during acute recovery, feeding tubes are placed without structured reassessment plans. In effect, interventions intended to be provisional too often become permanent because healthcare systems do not prioritize ongoing swallow evaluation and recovery-oriented follow-up [ 54 – 56 ]. Contemporary neuroplasticity-oriented dysphagia rehabilitation literature emphasizes the importance of active swallowing, task-specific practice, and physiologically targeted intervention during recovery [ 40 , 42 ]. Excessive reliance on strict non-oral nutrition without structured swallowing rehabilitation that includes therapeutic oral intake may therefore contribute to persistent swallowing impairment through mechanisms of disuse [ 94 , 95 ]. While enteral nutrition may be medically necessary during acute recovery, ongoing reassessment and active rehabilitation remain essential to maximizing recovery potential. Studies examining post-acute populations demonstrate that many patients with oral intake restrictions, including many with G-tubes, no longer demonstrate clinically significant dysphagia when reassessed with swallowing imaging [ 81 , 85 , 96 ], suggesting that inadequate reassessment contributes to unnecessary long-term restrictions. These outcomes are often invisible to acute care clinicians, who rarely receive longitudinal feedback regarding swallowing recovery or long-term feeding tube status after discharge.

Another important consideration is that feeding tubes do not eliminate aspiration risk. Patients discharged with G-tubes continue to experience substantial rates of aspiration pneumonia and hospital readmission [ 55 ]. These observations reinforce that enteral nutrition decisions are risk-benefit assessments rather than definitive solutions to aspiration risk. The relationship between dysphagia and pneumonia is complex and influenced by factors beyond aspiration alone, including oral health and hygiene, airway protection, foregut function, immune status, medical comorbidity, and overall functional status. Oral intake restriction may be appropriate when swallowing imaging demonstrates unsafe physiology; however, it should not be viewed as a default or permanent intervention without ongoing reassessment and rehabilitation [ 68 ]. Clear documentation regarding swallowing prognosis, rehabilitation goals, and plans for reassessment should accompany enteral nutrition decisions, and repeat swallowing imaging should be incorporated into post-discharge care pathways whenever possible.

The complexity of enteral nutrition decisions extends beyond medical risk alone. Eating and drinking carry profound personal, social, and cultural significance for many patients. Stroke survivors frequently describe loss of eating and drinking as one of the most psychologically devastating consequences of their stroke [ 97 , 98 ]. Dysphagia may be experienced not only as a loss of nutritional independence, but also as social isolation, loss of pleasure, and erosion of personal identity. Consequently, nutritional decisions should not be viewed solely through the lens of aspiration prevention, but also through their effects on autonomy, participation, and quality of life.

Recognizing the central role of eating and drinking in quality of life requires clinicians to engage patient autonomy as a core component of oral intake and nutrition decisions. In a prospective study of hospitalized stroke patients, two-thirds reported that long-term tube dependence on tube feeding would be equivalent to or worse than death [ 99 ]. Ethical obligations in dysphagia management, therefore, extend beyond risk reduction and include supporting informed patient decision-making when preferences, quality of life, and medical recommendations intersect.

For patients with severe dysphagia, poor overall prognosis, substantial comorbidity, or limited likelihood of meaningful recovery, comfort feeding (i.e., eating and drinking with an informed consent of risk or ‘feeding at risk’) represents an ethically grounded and clinically acceptable option that prioritizes dignity and patient-defined quality of life. Structured comfort-feeding pathways in non-stroke populations have been shown to be feasible and acceptable, with improvements in care processes and staff–patient communication [ 100 ]. Whether similar pathways improve patient-centered outcomes in severe post-stroke dysphagia warrants further investigation. Nevertheless, comfort-feeding discussions should be recognized as an important component of patient-centered dysphagia care and shared decision-making after stroke.

From Acute Diagnosis to Longitudinal Recovery: Improving Continuity, Reassessment, and Rehabilitation Access After Stroke Although critical decisions regarding swallowing management are often made during acute hospitalization, recovery from post-stroke dysphagia extends far beyond the inpatient setting. Increasingly, the literature identifies systems-level gaps in continuity of care, communication, reassessment, and rehabilitation access as major contributors to long-term dysphagia morbidity after stroke [ 53 – 56 ]. Contemporary guidelines similarly emphasize the need for coordinated interdisciplinary communication and patient and care partner education; however, they provide no guidance regarding optimal timing for reassessment or ongoing post-acute swallowing rehabilitation [ 2 , 56 , 101 , 102 ]. Given the influence of acute hospitalization on long-term swallowing outcomes, discharge planning should extend beyond immediate safety concerns and include explicit consideration of recovery potential, rehabilitation goals, and plans for longitudinal follow-up.

For many stroke survivors, discharge from acute hospitalization marks the beginning of an inconsistent and fragmented process for ongoing assessment and management of swallowing impairment. The quality and continuity of dysphagia care often varies considerably across inpatient rehabilitation facilities, skilled nursing facilities, outpatient services, and home-based care. Each of these settings operates within different resource constraints and may have variable access to clinicians with expertise in dysphagia assessment, swallowing imaging, and rehabilitation. As a result, opportunities for recovery may depend as much on post-acute service access rather as on swallowing impairment severity.

Access to swallowing imaging after acute discharge remains particularly variable. Patients receiving care in settings with established dysphagia care pathways and ready access to VFSS or FEES may be better positioned to undergo timely reassessment than those in settings where imaging is difficult to obtain because of transportation barriers, scheduling delays, and care coordination challenges. Yet reassessment, with swallowing imaging, should not be viewed as an optional component of care. Because swallowing function frequently changes during recovery, repeat swallowing imaging is often necessary to evaluate recovery, refine rehabilitation goals, guide oral intake advancement, and determine whether enteral nutrition remains necessary. Regardless of discharge disposition, reassessment should be recognized as an expected component of recovery-oriented dysphagia management rather than a service limited to higher resourced environments.

Communication across care settings represents another major challenge. Information transfer between acute care hospitals, rehabilitation facilities, outpatient providers, home health teams, patients, and care partners is frequently incomplete or inconsistent [ 3 , 50 , 103 ]. As a result, swallowing recommendations may be continued without understanding the physiologic rationale underlying them. Patients may undergo redundant evaluations, receive conflicting recommendations, or remain on unnecessarily restricted oral intake because updated swallowing information is unavailable. These inconsistencies may also erode trust among patients and care partners who receive differing recommendations without clear explanations.

Improving continuity will require more standardized communication regarding swallowing assessment findings and rehabilitation plans. Discharge documentation should clearly describe swallowing physiology, the rationale underlying oral intake recommendations, compensatory strategies that were trialed and their outcomes, anticipated recovery potential, and the recommended timing for reassessment. Whenever possible, swallowing imaging reports and access to recorded examinations should accompany patients during transitions between care settings. Such information may reduce redundant testing, improve continuity of care, and facilitate more individualized and effective rehabilitation planning.

Patients and care partners likewise require greater support in navigating post-stroke dysphagia recovery. Many families remain unaware that swallowing recovery may continue long after discharge or require repeat evaluation [ 103 ]. For patients discharged with G-tubes, additional burdens often fall upon patients, families, and care partners who must manage enteral feeding equipment despite having no prior experience. Acute care teams can help address these challenges through structured education and anticipatory guidance emphasizing the dynamic nature of swallowing recovery, the potential need for reassessment, and the importance of ongoing rehabilitation participation.

Access to skilled dysphagia rehabilitation represents another important systems-level challenge. Health system structures, reimbursement policies, and regulatory requirements substantially influence access to both swallowing rehabilitation and repeat swallowing imaging across post-acute care settings [ 80 – 84 ]. In many healthcare systems, documentation generated during acute hospitalization serves as the foundation for establishing medical necessity and authorizing services. Swallowing imaging findings, dysphagia severity classifications, oral intake recommendations, and documentation of functional limitations may therefore determine whether patients receive swallowing rehabilitation and reassessment. Failure to accurately identify and characterize swallowing impairment may limit access to recovery-oriented services long after the patient leaves the hospital. Greater alignment between reimbursement structures, quality oversight mechanisms, and evidence-based dysphagia management practices may help reduce disparities in access to recovery-oriented care. Organized interdisciplinary stroke systems have consistently been associated with improved patient outcomes, underscoring the value of coordinated rehabilitation pathways and continuity across the recovery continuum [ 10 ]. Ultimately, improving outcomes after stroke requires recognizing that dysphagia management does not end at hospital discharge. Post-stroke dysphagia should not be viewed solely as a short-term inpatient safety issue, but rather as a dynamic rehabilitation condition requiring longitudinal management, structured reassessment, coordinated communication, and equitable access to rehabilitation services (Figure). What occurs during acute hospitalization profoundly influences the trajectory of recovery, with long-term outcomes ultimately dependent upon whether patients can access the reassessment, rehabilitation, and support necessary to translate recovery potential into meaningful functional improvement (Fig. 1 ).

Dysphagia management begins during acute stroke hospitalization with identification of swallowing impairment and early clinical decisions regarding assessment, oral intake, rehabilitation, and nutritional support. Although these decisions are made during a brief hospitalization, they often influence long-term swallowing outcomes. Follow-up after discharge may be variable, underscoring the need for recovery-oriented care pathways that support reassessment, rehabilitation, and continuity of care across the stroke recovery continuum

Limitations and Future Directions Several limitations of the current evidence base warrant consideration. Much of the literature informing post-stroke dysphagia management derives from observational studies, registry analyses, retrospective cohorts, and expert consensus. Although these data consistently support the importance of dysphagia identification and management after stroke, high-quality prospective studies evaluating optimal timing of reassessment, swallowing imaging utilization, enteral feeding decisions, and post-acute care pathways remain limited. As a result, many aspects of contemporary dysphagia care continue to rely on extrapolation from heterogeneous populations and healthcare systems. Additional research is needed to better define recovery trajectories, identify patients most likely to benefit from specific rehabilitation approaches, and evaluate systems-level interventions designed to improve continuity of care. Future studies should also examine the effects of structured reassessment pathways, access to swallowing imaging across care settings, and patient-centered outcomes including quality of life, autonomy, and long-term feeding tube dependence.

Conclusion Post-stroke dysphagia remains an underrecognized determinant of stroke recovery and long-term health. Evidence increasingly supports recovery-oriented management including timely swallowing imaging, longitudinal reassessment, individualized rehabilitation, and coordinated transitions across care settings. Several priorities emerge from the current evidence. First, swallowing imaging should be recognized as a foundational component of post-stroke dysphagia management because accurate characterization of swallowing physiology is essential for diagnosis, rehabilitation planning, prognostication, and nutritional decision-making. Second, oral intake recommendations, restrictions, and decisions regarding enteral nutrition should account for the dynamic nature of swallowing recovery. Given the uncertainty of early prognostication, recovery-oriented care should avoid unnecessary long-term restrictions and support timely reassessment of patients with feeding tubes, including those who may ultimately recover sufficient swallowing function to permit G-tube removal. Third, systems of care must better support continuity across acute and post-acute settings through coordinated communication, structured reassessment pathways, patient and care partner education, and equitable access to rehabilitation and repeat swallow imaging. Many barriers to optimal outcomes reflect systems-level limitations rather than patient-level factors. A fundamental challenge in post-stroke dysphagia management is that many of the most consequential decisions regarding swallowing, nutrition, and rehabilitation are made during a hospitalization measured in days, whereas meaningful swallowing recovery often unfolds over months. Reframing post-stroke dysphagia as a rehabilitation condition requiring longitudinal management represents an important opportunity to better align stroke systems of care with the realities of recovery and improve long-term outcomes after stroke.

Stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is one of the most frequent complications after acute stroke, affecting approximately one in eight stroke patients. Besides prolonged hospitalisation and increased healthcare costs, it is also a major risk factor for mortality and poor functional recovery. The pathophysiology of SAP is driven by two converging processes: impaired local airway defence due to dysphagia as well as reduced airway clearance reflexes, and systemic stroke-induced immunodepression driven by dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system. While post-stroke immunodepression is a major risk factor for SAP, it might limit unwanted autoimmune responses within the brain. Conversely, SAP itself may drive neuroinflammation and contribute to post-stroke cognitive impairment. Despite its clinical importance, high-quality evidence to guide practice on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of SAP remains scarce and guideline recommendations are mostly based on expert consensus. Diagnosis of SAP is suggested to be based on standardised clinical criteria supported by chest radiography and C-reactive protein as an adjunct where uncertainty persists. After diagnosis, guidelines suggest prompt empirical antibiotic therapy according to local protocols. In contrast, preventive antibiotics, even for high-risk patients, neither improve clinical outcome nor reduce SAP frequency. Currently recommended preventive strategies for SAP therefore mostly focus on dysphagia management and early mobilisation. This review integrates the pathophysiology, long-term consequences of SAP and further research directions based on the current knowledge on post-stroke immunology with prevention, diagnosis and treatment of SAP as set out in the recent European Stroke Organisation guideline and related guidelines.

Nearly one in four people will be affected by stroke in their lifetime [ 2 ]. Beyond the immediate consequences of brain damage, oedema and cardiovascular complications, stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is an important complication after stroke. It can lead to respiratory failure and prolonged hospital stay, and it significantly contributes to mortality and worse functional recovery [ 3 – 5 ]. Current research also mechanistically links post-stroke infections to post-stroke cognitive impairment [ 6 ].

Although the clinical relevance of SAP has long been recognised, the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) published the first guideline on SAP in 2026 [ 4 ]. This guideline covers 15 PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions centred around diagnosis, treatment and prevention of SAP developing within 7 days after stroke onset and without need for mechanical ventilation. However, due to limited evidence, most recommendations are based on expert consensus statements (hereafter referred to as “suggestions”) rather than on reliable evidence (hereafter referred to as “recommendations”) from randomised controlled trials or informative systematic reviews [ 4 ].

In this narrative review, we summarize the current mechanistical immunological knowledge about post-stroke immunodepression and SAP and link it to clinical SAP management integrating the recently published ESO guideline on SAP [ 4 ] with the PISCES criteria [ 7 ], the BTS statement on aspiration pneumonia [ 8 ] and the German AWMF guideline on nosocomial pneumonia [ 9 ], as well as the ESO guideline on post-stroke dysphagia [ 10 ]. Additionally, we identify and discuss potential strategies for mechanism-based therapeutic targets and their limitations.

We conducted searches in the MEDLINE database until July 9, 2026 using the term “Stroke-associated Pneumonia” and complementary searches using combination of the term “Stroke” with “Infection” or “Pneumonia” with different filters (article type, publication date). Search results were screened on title/abstract level and (if necessary) in full text to identify relevant clinical or preclinical trials or recent systematic reviews published in peer-reviewed journals in full text that match the scope of this review. Additionally, we reviewed current guidelines as well as other current systematic reviews with thematic overlap and screened their reference lists for relevant articles.

Epidemiology SAP is defined as the spectrum of lower respiratory tract infections with onset within 7 days after stroke [ 11 ] – most commonly around day 3 [ 12 ]. Approximately one in eight stroke patients develop SAP [ 13 ] – far more than in other hospitalised patients (1.6%) [ 14 ]. However, incidence rates show some variation between stroke units [ 15 ] and a high degree of heterogeneity between studies [ 5 ], potentially due to differences in stroke unit management or in diagnostic criteria [ 16 ]. The consequences of SAP are severe: Along with other risk factors like stroke severity, age, delay in treatment and comorbidities [ 17 ], SAP is one of the major determinants of unfavourable stroke outcome [ 3 , 4 , 13 , 18 ]. In-patient mortality of stroke patients with SAP is 21.6% and severe stroke patients with SAP have – compared to severe stroke patients without SAP – about 40% increased risk of in-hospital mortality [ 3 , 13 ]. Besides increased mortality and unfavourable functional outcome, SAP is associated with higher economic burden, higher institutionalisation rates, prolonged hospital stay, prolonged intensive care stay, respiratory failure and recurrent stroke [ 4 , 18 – 20 ].

While dysphagia is the most important clinical risk factor for SAP, both dysphagia and SAP risk correlate with stroke severity [ 21 – 23 ]: While patients with a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) Score of ≤ 4 have a pneumonia risk of 1–2%, comparable to other hospitalised patients, this increases to about 28% in patients with NIHSS ≥ 16 [ 21 ]. But also age, male sex, prestroke disability and prestroke medical conditions (e.g. COPD) are risk factors [ 22 ].

There is limited high-quality data on causative pathogens in SAP. Microbiological analysis suggests a distinct pathogen spectrum than community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) or hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP): Most prevalent pathogens isolated from SAP patients were Gram-negative bacilli and Gram-positive cocci, especially Klebsiella pneumoniae , Staphylococcus aureus , Escherichia coli , Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii – while Streptococcus pneumoniae was only detected in 3.5% of cases and anaerobic bacteria were not detected or reported [ 24 ]. While respiratory viruses can be detected in up to 29% of CAP [ 25 ], their relevance in SAP remains unclear. Viral infections themselves, like influenza and SARS-CoV-2, however, increase stroke risk [ 26 ].

Pathophysiology of SAP The pathophysiology of SAP is driven by physical disabilities and immunodepression after stroke (Fig. 1 ) [ 4 , 18 ]. Dysphagia, reduced consciousness and reduced airway clearance mechanisms like coughing promote aspiration. Beyond aspiration, a gut-derived route for bacterial translocation to the lung has also been proposed in preclinical [ 27 ] and observational studies [ 28 ] based on findings that the microbiome composition changes in stroke and these changes are associated with SAP. However, other murine evidence argues against a causal relationship between gut bacterial overgrowth in stroke and stroke associated infection [ 29 ]. Given that dysphagia is the main risk factor for SAP and based on microbiological data, however, the ESO guideline assumes SAP to be more closely related to aspiration pneumonia [ 4 ]. Nevertheless, the microbiome is an important modifier of the immune composition also in the context of stroke [ 30 – 32 ].

Aspiration alone, however, cannot account for SAP since micro-aspiration is common in healthy individuals without leading to pneumonia [ 33 ] and massive aspiration is rare in stroke patients [ 4 ]. Animal studies have shown increased susceptibility to pneumonia after bacterial exposure in stroke animals compared to sham-operated animals [ 34 ].

A degree of systemic immunodepression is also described in other CNS injuries [ 35 ] and non-neurological severe diseases like myocardial infarction [ 36 ]. In stroke, cell damage and hypoxia-associated stress cause a local neuroinflammation within the brain that also shapes the systemic immune response in an infarct-size dependent manner [ 37 , 38 ]. Damaged inhibitory pathways and local cytokines such as IL-1β and TNFα cause activation of the sympathetic nervous system, the vagal nerve and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA-) axis [ 18 ]. Additionally, proinflammatory mediators directly released by the brain, like HMGB1, have the potential to shape the systemic immune response [ 39 ].

The sympathetic nervous system activation with the release of catecholamines into the bloodstream and lymphoid organs starts as early as hours after stroke [ 40 , 41 ]. In the spleen of mice after experimental stroke, this leads to a loss of marginal-zone B cells and a reduction of systemic IgM, mediated by sympathetic beta-receptors [ 42 ]. Human stroke patients show reduced monocytic HLA-DR expression (important for antigen presentation and adaptive immune response) and impaired oxidative burst in monocytes within hours after stroke onset [ 40 , 43 , 44 ], which was associated with elevated norepinephrine levels and susceptibility to post-stroke infections [ 40 ].

Glucocorticoid release from the adrenal gland, mediated via the HPA-axis, might further contribute to lymphopenia via reduced lymphopoiesis [ 45 ] and additionally suppresses the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [ 46 ] – further aggravated by direct activation of efferent vagal nerve fibres in stroke [ 47 ]. In mouse experiments, local immunodepression in the lung was also shaped by activation of acetylcholine receptors on alveolar macrophages and epithelial cells [ 48 ]. Additional effects of stroke on mucociliary clearance are still being investigated.

Beyond reduced antigen presentation molecules on monocytes, patients with stroke show lymphopenia affecting B cells and various T cell subsets like CD4 + , CD8 + or γδ T cells together with transient atrophy of lymphoid organs [ 37 , 41 , 49 – 53 ]. Further changes include lower proinflammatory and higher anti-inflammatory cytokine levels in the blood and a long-lasting shift in T cell phenotype from Th1 (proinflammatory) to Th2 (anti-inflammatory) [ 37 , 41 , 49 – 53 ]. Reductions in CD4 + T cells are particularly associated with SAP [ 49 ].

In neutrophils, particularly important for the antibacterial defence in the lung, key functions in defence against micro-organisms like oxidative burst or NET (neutrophil extracellular traps) formation might be impaired and anti-inflammatory subsets of neutrophils increased [ 54 – 56 ]. At the same time, neutrophil counts rise in the blood in the first days after stroke and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio increases [ 54 ] - this ratio and neutrophil numbers perform as a predictive biomarker for SAP [ 4 , 57 ].

Stroke occurs mainly in older individuals and age is a risk factor for the development of SAP [ 22 ]. Ageing is accompanied by a chronic low-grade inflammatory state and by a functional decline of the innate and adaptive immune responses [ 58 ]. In stroke, higher levels of Th17-like cells and higher neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios as well as changes in B cell subsets were observed in aged individuals [ 58 ]. In preclinical studies, reduced neutrophil invasion and phagocytotic capacity in the lung as well as intestinal inflammation with disruption in gut barriers were proposed to contribute to the increased SAP risk of older patients [ 59 , 60 ]. Currently, however, age-stratified immunological studies in patients with SAP are lacking.

SAP and long-term consequences The risk of dementia after stroke is already higher than in the general population [ 61 ] and might be aggravated by systemic inflammation, e.g. due to infections, like SAP (Fig. 1 ) [ 6 , 62 ]. Post-stroke cognitive impairment occurs especially in the first year after stroke and hazard ratios are higher in haemorrhagic stroke, severe stroke and in younger patients (though absolute risks are higher in older patients) [ 61 , 63 , 64 ]. While the exact link between stroke and dementia is yet to be elucidated, there is growing evidence that inflammatory mechanisms in the brain contribute to dementia risk [ 6 ]. Possible mechanisms include production of proinflammatory cytokines after phagocytosis [ 65 ], Toll-like receptor 4 signalling [ 66 ], and adaptive immune responses with B and T cell driven autoreactivity to CNS antigens [ 67 – 69 ]. Post-stroke immunodepression might be helpful to avoid these consequences. The strength of the early immune response two days after stroke correlated with worse functional outcome after 3 months and 1 year [ 70 ]. On the other hand, infectious triggers can stimulate autoreactive responses and thereby contribute to worse outcome after stroke [ 71 , 72 ]. Infections might also push microglia towards a proinflammatory and neurodegenerative phenotype or can enhance leukocyte trafficking to the CNS by damaging the integrity of the blood-brain-barrier [ 6 , 73 , 74 ].

Thus, while post-stroke immunodepression is an important risk factor for infections after stroke and thereby exerts negative effects on stroke outcome, in the absence of infection post-stroke immunodepression might contribute to better stroke outcome by limiting excessive neuroinflammation [ 18 , 75 ]. This immunodepression dilemma limits the clinical applicability of past experimental findings and underscores the need to balance these divergent effects carefully.

Diagnosis In general, stroke unit care including a daily clinical assessment is recommended for all patients after stroke [ 4 ]. Currently, there is no generally accepted gold standard in the diagnosis of SAP, which also complicates efforts to establish new diagnostic principles [ 4 ]. Both clinical algorithms like the mCDC-criteria and physician-diagnosed pneumonia showed high specificity but only moderate sensitivity and still tend to over-diagnose SAP [ 76 ]. However, diagnosis of SAP using mCDC-criteria had better positive predictive value and better agreement; it might be better at discriminating clinically relevant pneumonia that is associated with poor outcome and requires antibiotic treatment from isolated signs of infection without need for antibiotic treatment caused e.g. by aspiration pneumonitis [ 76 , 77 ]. Therefore, the ESO suggests using algorithm-based approaches like the PISCES (Pneumonia in Stroke Consensus Group)-modified CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) -criteria [ 11 ] to establish the diagnosis of probable SAP in the absence of typical radiological findings in the two serial chest radiographs and the diagnosis of confirmed SAP when typical radiological signs are present (Table 1 ) [ 4 ].

Chest X-ray remains the first-line imaging modality but was shown to have limited diagnostic value and weak inter-rater reliability [ 78 ]. Therefore, computed tomography (CT) may be considered for situations with diagnostic uncertainty and therapeutic consequence [ 4 ]. Conversely, despite first promising attempts of lung ultrasound in a small cohort [ 79 ], there is yet insufficient evidence for the ESO to recommend its use routinely [ 4 ].

Retrospective analyses showed good sensitivity and specificity for different CRP-values, especially in combination with chest and laboratory findings – also in afebrile patients, although each cut-off traded sensitivity against specificity and moderate CRP elevations are also observed in stroke without infection [ 76 , 80 ]. A CRP-cutoff value of 30–40 mg/L may be useful, especially in case of diagnostic uncertainty particularly in afebrile patients [ 4 ]. Future concepts of diagnosis might also include ex vivo synthesized cytokines from patients´ blood samples that might serve as biomarkers for SAP [ 81 ]. Following the principles of antibiotic stewardship, microbial diagnostics with sputum and blood cultures, as well as urinary antigen testing for Streptococcus pneumoniae or Legionella species are suggested, especially in severe cases [ 4 ].

Therapy Once the diagnosis of a probable or a confirmed SAP is established, empiric antibiotic therapy is suggested to be initiated as soon as possible [ 4 ]. While previously, the PISCES group suggested starting antibiotic therapy within 4 h after diagnosis [ 7 ], recent data and guidelines do not support this strict threshold but rather suggest timely administration, as soon as feasible for the individual patient [ 4 , 82 , 83 ]. In patients with sepsis (about 2% of stroke patients), immediate treatment (< 3 h, < 1 h for septic shock) is crucial for patient survival – mortality risk increases in septic shock patients by 4% with every hour of delay [ 84 – 86 ].

The empiric choice of antibiotic agent is suggested to be tailored to local protocols considering resistance patterns and patient risk factors [ 4 , 7 ]. Previously, PISCES suggested CAP-treatment for SAP developing in the first 3 days after stroke [ 7 ]. As the bacterial spectrum shows overlap with aspiration pneumonia and some overlap with hospital-acquired pneumonia – even in the first 72 h after stroke – treatment is now suggested by the ESO guideline accordingly [ 4 ]. Table 2 summarises a choice of antibiotic agents and dosages for SAP treatment according to ESO SAP guideline, PISCES SAP recommendations, BTS aspiration pneumonia guideline and AWMF guideline on nosocomial pneumonia [ 4 , 7 – 9 ]. Treatment options compatible with these guidelines are e.g. amoxicillin with clavulanic acid. Alternative options include third- or fourth-generation fluoroquinolones, like levofloxacin or moxifloxacin (if beta-lactam antibiotics cannot be used), or amoxicillin plus metronidazole [ 4 , 7 , 8 ]. Where risk factors for MRSA are present, vancomycin or linezolid might be added, whereas suspected ESBL-producing organisms require carbapenems [ 4 , 7 ]. Aspiration pneumonitis – a rare chemical injury caused by aspiration of large volumes of gastric contents – needs to be distinguished from SAP: Here, antibiotic treatment may only be started if bacterial infection becomes evident after 24–48 h – then, atypical pathogens and anaerobes need to be considered [ 4 , 8 ]. In a stable clinical situation and as soon as feasible in the context of possible dysphagia, intravenous antibiotic therapy should be switched to oral therapy [ 4 ]. In a retrospective analysis, macrolide treatment (not routinely recommended for SAP treatment) was associated with better functional outcome for pneumonia after stroke while other antibiotic agents exerted negative effects, which may point towards immune-modulatory effects but limitations of the retrospective trial design apply [ 4 , 87 ]. For pneumonia developing beyond 7 days after stroke antibiotic treatment is suggested to follow HAP guidelines [ 7 ].

The length of antibiotic treatment has been subject of intense debates recently [ 88 ]. Previously, longer courses of antibiotic treatment were preferred in the belief that pathogens had to be eradicated completely to avoid resistance [ 89 ]. In the light of new evidence that every single dose of antibiotics can cause side effects [ 90 ], evoke resistance [ 91 ] and that antibiotic therapy can alter the microbiome and thereby impair lung defence mechanisms [ 31 , 92 ], this approach has shifted towards “shorter is better” [ 93 ]. Shortened courses have proven non-inferior and are associated with less treatment burden or fewer adverse events in other infectious diseases like CAP in adults [ 94 ] and children [ 95 ]. For inpatients with non-severe CAP, the American Thoracic Society Clinical Practice Guideline already recommends shortened antibiotic durations of 3–5 days [ 83 ]. For SAP, no randomised controlled trial has investigated the duration of antibiotic treatment; in a cohort study, however, the amount of antibiotics administered was independently associated with worse outcomes in infections after intracerebral haemorrhage [ 96 ]. The recent ESO guideline on SAP therefore suggests in a consensus-statement inspired by aspiration pneumonia guidance and HAP-guidelines [ 8 , 97 , 98 ] an antibiotic duration tailored to clinical course, but not shorter than 5 days [ 4 ]. In any case, the treatment should be re-evaluated after 48–72 h, adjusted to microbiological results and stopped immediately if the diagnosis is incorrect [ 4 , 9 ].

While continuous monitoring for hypoxia for the first 2–3 days may improve outcomes [ 99 ], supply of oxygen is only suggested for cases of hypoxia (target value: SpO 2 ≥ 94%) [ 4 , 100 ]. Here, the cause should be identified and treated causally [ 4 ]. Cough-assist devices or respiratory therapy might also be useful in the setting of a stroke unit on an individual basis, as well as early rehabilitation and respiratory muscle training [ 4 ].

Corticosteroids or paracetamol are not suggested for SAP prevention unless there is another clear indication [ 101 – 103 ]. Although elevated body temperature affects many stroke patients and is a risk factor for unfavourable outcome, fever management itself does not improve prognosis [ 104 ] .

Prevention Dysphagia is an important pathophysiological factor in the development of SAP, and is also (amongst others) a risk factor for malnutrition and prolonged hospital stay, and is associated with worse functional outcome and mortality [ 10 ]. Formal dysphagia screening can reduce pneumonia rates [ 105 ] and is recommended for all stroke patients before the oral intake of any food, liquids or medication (Table 3 ) [ 10 ]. Adherence to such basic measures varies in routine care but can be improved by supported implementation of nurse-initiated protocols [ 106 ]. In patients with clinical predictors of post-stroke dysphagia, a timely more comprehensive dysphagia assessment is recommended, comprising a clinical swallowing examination and, where indicated, instrumental assessment by flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) or videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS) [ 10 , 107 , 108 ]. Recommended treatment of dysphagia comprises texture-modified diets, fluid/nutritional monitoring with possibility of a nasogastric tube, oral health care and measures to rehabilitate swallowing function – such as swallowing exercises [ 10 ]. However, the role of structured oral hygiene in prevention of SAP, though feasible and safe, is not clear [ 4 , 109 ].

Several prediction scores are available to identify patients with stroke at increased risk of developing SAP, like the ISAN, A2DS2, AIS-APS, PANTHERIS, PASS [ 4 , 110 ]. Considering factors like age, NIHSS, GCS, sex, dysphagia, prestroke dependence, and prestroke medical conditions they achieve a moderate to good discriminatory performance that can be further modestly improved by biomarkers like PCTus, CRP, IL-6, neutrophils or neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [ 4 , 110 , 111 ]. Also radiological findings in CT scans upon admission might already detect early signs of SAP [ 112 ]. In the future, machine-learning approaches might further improve risk evaluation for SAP in stroke patients [ 113 ].

To date, however, the identification of at-risk patients for SAP has no therapeutic consequences in the absence of specific validated preventive treatment [ 4 ]. For bacterial infections, the most obvious prevention strategy is antibiotic treatment. In different large randomised controlled trials (PASS [ 114 ], STROKE-INF [ 115 ], PRECIOUS [ 103 ]), however, antibiotic therapy reduced urinary tract infections but did not reduce the rates of SAP and did not improve functional outcome after 90 days [ 4 , 116 ] – even when tailored to the biomarker PCT (STRAWINSKI-trial [ 117 ]).

As post-stroke immunodepression is largely mediated via the sympathetic nervous system and beta-receptors [ 18 ], beta-blockers might mitigate these effects and contribute to immune reconstitution. In animal experiments, beta-blockers in high dosages were able to reverse immunosuppressive effects after stroke [ 41 , 42 , 118 ]. However, adverse effects such as stronger autoreactive immune responses need to be taken into consideration [ 75 ]. Most studies on beta-blockers in stroke are observational and contained a large proportion of patients already treated with beta-blockers before: They showed no reduction in SAP rates for stroke patients treated with beta-blockers, though overall mortality was reduced [ 4 , 119 , 120 ]. Therefore, the ESO guideline does not suggest beta-blockers for prevention of SAP and suggests only continuing previous therapy or starting therapy for other reasons (Table 3 ) [ 4 ]. A randomised controlled trial on beta-blockers in intracerebral haemorrhage has just finished recruiting [ 121 ].

As stroke promotes gastro-oesophageal reflux and aspiration is a frequent cause of SAP, especially in patients with a nasogastric tube, gastric acid blockers or antiemetics were discussed as preventive strategy [ 4 ]. For prevention of pneumonia with metoclopramide, a randomised controlled trial is currently ongoing (ISRCTN40512746). However, previous studies showed inconclusive results on SAP and stroke outcome with antiemetics [ 4 , 122 – 125 ] and even association of higher SAP incidence with gastric acid blockers [ 126 ].

To exploit the disease-modifying properties of the microbiome some clinical studies tested selective decontamination of the digestive tract [ 127 ] and probiotics (combined with early enteral nutrition) [ 128 ] and report reduced pneumonia rates in stroke, but the trials are mostly small, confounded by dysphagia, have a high or unclear risk of bias, and SAP was rarely a predefined endpoint. For this reason, neither approach is recommended yet.

While Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) reduced pneumonia rates and lowered mortality in some studies, they did not show benefits in functional outcome [ 129 ]. Benzodiazepines [ 130 ] did not show benefit at all and data on statins is contradictory with potential benefit on SAP prevention [ 4 , 131 , 132 ]. Due to the limited evidence, ACEIs, ARBs, benzodiazepines or statins should be applied according to their primary indications and are not suggested for SAP prevention (Table 3 ) [ 4 ]. Also, the mode of gastric feeding (continuous vs. intermittent) does not seem to have influence on SAP rates [ 4 ].

Generally, however, the ESO suggests respiratory muscle training and pulmonary rehabilitation for SAP prevention. Also, early mobilisation within 48 h after stroke and even passive mobilisation are recommended to reduce SAP risk (Table 3 ) [ 4 , 133 – 135 ] – though prolonged very early out-of-bed mobilisation (< 24 h after stroke) is associated with slightly more deaths and poorer outcome in severe stroke patients and should therefore be avoided in these patients [ 4 , 136 ]. Furthermore, for SAP prevention the ESO guideline suggests that patients should be positioned in a 30–45 degree head-up position during and after enteral feeding and, on the basis of a small study, to turn patients with reduced level of consciousness from supine to the right and left lateral recumbent position during the daytime every 2 h when they cannot change their position themselves [ 4 ].

Future directions Stroke-associated pneumonia is a frequent complication after stroke and one of the main determinants of mortality and outcome [ 3 , 4 ]. It affects about 12% of stroke patients and is caused by dysphagia, impairment of respiratory muscles and coughing reflexes, immobilisation and a general immunodepression after stroke that in particular also affects local defence against pathogens in the lung [ 4 , 13 , 18 ].

Diagnosis is suggested to be based on clinical scores, like the modified clinical CDC-criteria for probable SAP and additional radiographic signs for confirmed SAP and may be complemented by CRP values [ 4 ]. Once the diagnosis of a probable or confirmed SAP is established, empiric antibiotic treatment is suggested to be started immediately according to local standards, for example with amoxicillin/clavulanate and to be continued for generally at least 5 days depending on the clinical course [ 4 , 7 , 8 ].

Although there are moderate to good scores for defining patients at risk for SAP, there are currently no specific effective strategies for the pharmacological prevention of SAP – most importantly, the ESO recommends against the use of preventive antibiotic therapy [ 4 ]. Exercise, dysphagia management and mobilisation might reduce pneumonia rates, but are also beneficial for stroke outcome in any case and should therefore be available to all stroke patients [ 4 ].

Several explanations have been proposed for the absence of a protective effect of preventive antibiotic treatment [ 4 ]: (1) Antibiotic coverage might not have been adequate – although the antibiotics used (ceftriaxone and co-amoxiclav/clarithromycin) should have covered all relevant pathogens [ 24 ]. (2) The open label design might have led to increased antibiotic prescription in the control group – but antibiotic prescription was in total still higher in the intervention arms [ 114 , 115 ]. (3) In already good stroke unit care there might be little room for improvement in stroke outcome – which appears unlikely due to prevalence and mortality rates of SAP [ 3 , 4 , 13 ]. (4) As preclinical evidence suggests an early beginning of SAP within hours after stroke [ 34 ] and signs of pneumonia are already present in CT upon admission to hospital [ 112 ], the mean antibiotic start in the trials 24 h after stroke could have been too late – this would however also question the value of early antibiotic therapy after diagnosis of SAP. (5) The current clinical scores and diagnostic criteria might mainly define other lung diseases or infections as SAP – this would also call into question the necessity of antibiotic treatment for non-severe SAP.

The new ESO guideline for SAP gives recommendations and suggestions on 15 important questions regarding diagnosis, therapy and prevention of SAP [ 4 ]. However, most studies on SAP are observational and partly confounded by stroke severity and end-of-life decisions. The guideline reports that only for a minority of 3 PICO-defined questions, (mostly weak) clinical evidence was available for an evidence-based recommendation rather than an expert-consensus based suggestion, underscoring the need for high-quality clinical trials. Especially questions of antibiotic therapy choice and duration as well as additional drugs and interventions remain unanswered. Diagnostic accuracy studies are currently limited by the lack of an available gold standard and pneumonia severity scores have not been systematically validated for SAP. Also, prevention strategies need to be developed especially for high-risk populations in the light of mechanistic and microbiological insights [ 4 ]. Latest clinical trials mainly focused on dysphagia treatment for SAP prevention [ 137 – 140 ].

With the establishment of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) over the last decade, other risk factors may additionally need to be considered: Besides admission NIHSS, also NIHSS after 24 h and the procedural time of EVT were identified as predictors of SAP in different observational studies [ 57 , 141 , 142 ]. Also EVT itself has been described as a risk factor for SAP [ 143 , 144 ], possibly due to procedural factors like general anaesthesia, ventilation and delayed extubation [ 145 – 147 ] – a recent RCT found lower SAP rates (but not statistically significant) when comparing early with delayed extubation [ 148 ].

Future research will need to investigate further local and systemic pathophysiological mechanisms of SAP to identify possible drug targets. Beta-blockers or systemic Interferon-γ might be able to mitigate effects of systemic post-stroke immunodepression but might also promote autoreactive immune reactions within the brain [ 40 – 42 ]. On the other hand, immunomodulatory treatments that might alleviate stroke damage need to be balanced against SAP risk in the periphery ultimately leading to an unfavourable outcome [ 18 , 149 ]. Other future treatment targets include Granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and CD200 receptor 1 signalling, which showed positive effects in the brain after experimental stroke and might reduce SAP risk [ 150 , 151 ]. Also, treatment with IgM-enriched intravenous immunoglobulins improved bacterial clearance from the lung after experimental stroke but did not affect infarct volume in preclinical studies [ 152 ], underscoring the need for future clinical trials on immunomodulatory therapies.

Preventive and immunomodulatory strategies have so far been tested in largely unselected stroke populations without success. Markers of post-stroke immunodepression (HLA-DR expression on monocytes, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio) and systemic inflammation biomarkers (CRP, IL-6 or usPCT) might help defining stroke patient cohorts with high risk of SAP but with potentially different underlying risk factors. Especially patients with low HLA-DR levels might benefit from GM-CSF treatment to restore immune function – like it has been shown for sepsis [ 153 ]. However, as infection might already start within a few hours after stroke, at a time when neuroinflammation is also increasing, timing might be critical for effective prevention of SAP and to balance SAP risk with possible autoreactive immune reactions in the brain.

Researchers should therefore test the hypothesis of an early closing therapeutic window for preventive SAP treatment, the possibility that preventive antibiotic therapy is only helpful in yet undefined very high risk populations [ 154 ] or the possibility of diagnosed SAP that is not caused by bacteria amenable to antibiotics. This also points out the need for evaluation of the microbiological pathogen spectrum, for robust and meaningful diagnostic frameworks including biomarkers, for new mechanism-driven approaches for immunomodulation and prevention, especially in high-risk patients, and for evaluation of existing and new antibiotic treatment strategies [ 4 ]. Especially immunomodulatory effects of different antibiotic classes and their implications for neuroinflammation need to be explored – also with regard to the gut microbiome that has increasingly been recognised as a modulator of neuroinflammatory processes after stroke [ 18 , 32 ] and might also affect lung pathology [ 31 , 92 ].

Research on SAP therefore not only needs to consider local processes in the airways and lung contributing to SAP: It needs to consider local and distant immunomodulatory processes and target the immunodepression dilemma with systemic immunodepression on the one side and possible neuroinflammatory and autoreactive effects within the brain in the chronic phase after stroke on the other side. Abstract Objective To evaluate the effects of oral hygiene care on swallowing-related outcomes in hospitalised patients with post-stroke dysphagia (PSD).

Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov up to May 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-RCTs with a comparison group that reporting swallowing-related outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for RCTs and ROBINS-I for non-RCTs. Where appropriate, meta-analyses were conducted using random-effects models to estimate mean differences (MDs), odds ratios (ORs) and risk differences (RDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.

Results Nine studies, comprising 7 RCTs and two non-RCTs, were included, with risk-of-bias ratings ranging from low risk to some concerns for RCTs and moderate risk for non-RCTs. Oral hygiene care increased the odds of achieving independent oral intake compared with usual care (OR = 2.54, 95% CI, 1.80; 3.59; I 2 = 0%), corresponding to a 13% absolute increase (RD = 0.13, 95% CI, 0.03; 0.23; I 2 = 0%). Functional Oral Intake Scale (FOIS; scores 1–7), with higher scores indicating more independent and unrestricted oral intake, favoured oral hygiene care (MD = 0.40, 95% CI, 0.07; 0.72; I 2 = 0%). Similarly, Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS; scores 0–20), assessing swallowing safety and dysphagia severity, favoured oral hygiene care (MD = 2.93, 95% CI, 1.01; 4.85; I 2 = 0%). The certainty of the evidence for achieving independent oral intake was rated as high.

Conclusion Oral hygiene care supports swallowing recovery in patients with PSD, particularly independent oral intake and should be considered an active component of dysphagia rehabilitation. Graphical abstract Graphical abstract Graphical abstract summarising a systematic review and meta-analysis of nine studies on oral hygiene care for hospitalised patients with post-stroke dysphagia. Compared with usual care, oral hygiene care increased the odds of achieving independent oral intake (odds ratio 2.54; risk difference 0.13). The certainty of evidence for this outcome was rated as high.

In hospital settings, oral hygiene care includes oral assessment, mechanical mouth cleaning such as toothbrushing and tongue cleaning, oral rinsing, oral moisturising, and denture care. 5 This care is recommended to reduce oral bacterial colonisation and support pneumonia prevention in high-risk hospitalised patients, including those with dysphagia. 3 , 5 , 6 In patients with PSD, aspiration of saliva or food residue contaminated with oral pathogens contributes to the development of stroke-associated pneumonia. 3 , 6

Swallowing recovery depends not only on oral muscle strength and coordination but also on adequate masticatory function, bolus formation, saliva function, oral comfort, and sensory input from the oral cavity and pharynx. 1 , 7–9 Several oral health and oral function factors, including functional dentition, occlusal support of posterior teeth, tongue coating, tongue strength, oral hygiene status, dry mouth, and food residue, have been associated with swallowing function, oral intake, or aspiration pneumonia risk in patients with stroke. 6–9 Oral hygiene care may support swallowing recovery by improving oral comfort and moisture, reducing oral residue and tongue coating, and facilitating more effective bolus formation. 7–9 In addition, oral hygiene care, including toothbrushing and/or oral stimulation, may provide mechanical and sensory input to the tongue, teeth, gingiva, and oral mucosa. This type of care can influence swallowing reflex pathways through oral and pharyngeal sensory afferents and may contribute to sensorimotor activation within the swallowing network. 10 , 11

Despite these biologically plausible mechanisms, evidence on whether oral hygiene care improves swallowing recovery in hospitalised patients with PSD has not been systematically synthesised, as existing research and clinical recommendations have largely focused on oral bacterial control and pneumonia prevention. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of oral hygiene care on swallowing-related outcomes in hospitalised patients with PSD.

Methods Protocol and registration The protocol for this systematic review and meta-analysis was prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number: CRD420261402713). This review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. 12

Search strategy Six electronic databases—MEDLINE via Ovid, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL)—and 1 trial registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, were searched from inception to 22 May 2026. Additional searches were conducted using forward and backward citation searching of studies that met the inclusion criteria. No date or language restrictions were applied. The search strategy included a combination of Medical Subject Headings and keywords related to the population, intervention, and outcomes: patients with stroke, oral hygiene, and swallowing-related outcomes, respectively. The full search strategy for each database is presented in Supplemental Material I .

Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (1) randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or non-RCTs with a comparison group; (2) inclusion of hospitalised patients with PSD during the acute and subacute phases of stroke, defined as within 6 months after stroke onset; (3) evaluation of oral hygiene; (4) reporting of swallowing-related outcomes; and (5) availability of the full text or study results in a trial registry.

Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers (S.P. and M.M.) independently screened all titles and abstracts, assessed full-text articles for final eligibility, and extracted data. Rayyan (Rayyan Intelligent Systematic Review; https://rayyan.ai ) was used to manage citations and facilitate independent, blinded screening and data extraction. Extracted data included study characteristics, population characteristics, intervention and comparator, swallowing recovery-related outcomes, and follow-up duration. When outcome data were incomplete or inconsistently reported, the authors were contacted for clarification. Studies were excluded if no response was received within 4 weeks and clarification was necessary to determine eligibility. For studies that appeared to meet the eligibility criteria but were published in languages other than English, translations were generated using DeepL.com , an AI-driven online translation tool. Disagreements at any stage of study selection or data extraction were resolved through discussion and consensus with the research team.

Risk of bias assessment and certainty of evidence Two reviewers (S.P. and M.M.) independently assessed the risk of bias and the certainty of the evidence. The Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, version 2 (RoB 2), was used for RCTs, whereas the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies—of Interventions, version 2 (ROBINS-I V2), was used for non-RCTs. The certainty of the evidence for each outcome was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. 13 The following GRADE domains were evaluated: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Evidence started as high certainty and was downgraded when concerns were identified in the GRADE domains. The certainty of the evidence was classified as high, moderate, low, or very low. Disagreements were resolved through consensus discussion.

Quantitative data analysis Random-effects meta-analyses were performed when at least two studies reported sufficiently comparable outcomes and provided adequate quantitative data for pooling. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic. Effect sizes were expressed as odds ratios (ORs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A pooled risk difference (RD) with a 95% CI was additionally calculated for dichotomous outcomes to provide an absolute measure of treatment effect. Statistical significance was set at p < .05. Subgroup analyses were conducted to examine whether the effects of oral hygiene care differed according to study design (RCT vs non-RCT), adjunctive intervention (with vs without adjunctive oral stimulation), follow-up period (1–2 weeks vs 3–4 weeks), and stroke phase (acute vs subacute) at participant recruitment. The RCT-only subgroup analysis was additionally used as a sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of the pooled effect. All analyses were conducted in RStudio using R version 4.5.0 and the meta package.

Results Description of included studies A PRISMA flowchart depicting the study selection process is shown in Figure 1 . After removing duplicates, 1201 records identified through the search strategy were screened. After title and abstract screening, 50 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. One additional study was identified through citation searching. Finally, 9 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis. An overview of excluded studies, including reasons for exclusion, is provided in Supplemental Material II . Figure 1 PRISMA 2020 flow diagram of study selection.

PRISMA 2020 flow diagram illustrating the study selection process. Database and register searches identified 2,281 records, of which 1,080 duplicates were removed and 1,201 records were screened. Backward and forward citation searches identified 685 and 555 records, respectively. Following screening and eligibility assessment, nine studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis.

Most studies were conducted in Asia, including China, 15 , 18 , 19 Taiwan, 16 , 17 and Thailand, 20 while 2 studies were conducted in the United States 14 , 21 and 1 in Denmark. 22 Two studies were translated from Chinese. 15 , 19 Publication years ranged from 2014 to 2026. Regarding outcome follow-up periods, 5 studies reported outcomes within 2 weeks or during hospitalisation, 14 , 17 , 18 , 20 , 21 while 4 studies reported outcomes at 3 to 4 weeks. 15 , 16 , 19 , 22

In terms of participant characteristics, 5 studies included participants with ischaemic stroke only or a majority of participants with ischaemic stroke, 16–20 while 4 studies did not classify stroke type. 14 , 15 , 21 , 22 Four studies recruited participants primarily during the acute phase, with recruitment occurring within 3 days after stroke onset, 15 , 17 , 18 , 21 whereas the other studies recruited participants during the subacute phase, defined as >7 days to 6 months after stroke. 14 , 16 , 19 , 20 , 22 Participants were generally older adults, with a higher proportion of males than females.

Risk of bias The risk-of-bias assessments of the included studies are summarised in Figure 2 . Among the 7 RCTs, three were judged to be at low risk of bias, 14 , 16 , 18 and 4 were judged to have some concerns. 15 , 17 , 19 , 20 Concerns were related to unclear randomisation processes 15 , 19 , 20 and non-blinding of the intervention group to the outcome assessors. 17 , 19 , 20 All non-RCTs were judged to be at moderate risk of bias due to potential confounding. 21 , 22 Across both study designs, risk of bias in the outcome measurement domain was judged according to the degree of assessor judgement involved and whether outcome assessors were blinded. Outcomes requiring clinical judgement (eg, clinically assessed oral intake status) were considered more susceptible to assessor bias, whereas more objective outcomes, such as tube feeding status, were considered less susceptible to assessor influence.

Data synthesis and meta-analysis Effects on swallowing function and oral intake outcomes Within the swallowing function and oral intake outcomes, 3 outcomes were identified, all of which were included in meta-analyses ( Figure 3 ): (1) independent oral intake (yes/no) based on clinical swallowing tests 14 , 15 and tube feeding status; 16 , 20 , 22 (2) Functional Oral Intake Scale (FOIS) score, which represents the level of oral intake from 1 to 7, where 1 indicates total tube dependence and 7 indicates independent oral intake without restrictions; and (3) Gugging Swallowing Screen (GUSS) score, which assesses swallowing safety and dysphagia severity from 0 to 20, with higher scores indicating better swallowing function. Achieving independent oral intake was used as the primary outcome because it is clinically meaningful and was the outcome most frequently available for pooling, whereas the other outcomes were considered secondary outcomes.
